submission.natural_language_explanation: The pole fires on the token that completes a multi-word unit, not on the token's identity: the last element of a compound name or pre-modified bare NP ('British scientists' 1.63 vs 'The scientists' 0.00; 'Golden State Warriors' 1.69 then 2.64), the second token of a fixed multiword preposition ('according to' 1.77, 'compared with' 0.39 vs 'compared to' 0.21), a separator that closes a dateline/header ('MANILA (Reuters) -' 3.26 vs the same slot filled by a comma 0.62), a complementizer or connective that closes the matrix clause ('ruled that' 0.30, 'five, then' 0.44, 'half, and' 0.59), and the period or newline that ends a sentence or paragraph (peak 0.5-1.8 in about 40% of the corpus's declarative sentences, 0.00-0.14 in the rest). It stays near zero on the same surface tokens when they open rather than close a unit (a comma in the dateline slot, 'ruled:' 0.13, the first element 'British' 0.03, interior content words after the unit closes), and the whole completed span must be present: ablating any single content word inside it drops the peak by 60-90%.

adversarial_test_results.prompt:
DAKAR (Reuters) - When the first boreholes were drilled outside the village of Ndiaganiao, few in the district expected the water to last through the dry season. Two years later, the pumps still run every morning, and the queues at the standpipes have shortened enough that women no longer walk before dawn to reach them first.

Local engineers attribute the change to a modest rehabilitation programme that replaced corroded pipes, sealed the wellheads and trained a dozen residents to carry out routine repairs. The work cost roughly 40 million CFA francs, a sum that would have covered barely a kilometre of new road.

Not every village has fared as well. In the neighbouring commune of Sessene, a similar scheme stalled after the contractor withdrew, and the old hand pumps now sit idle beside a water tower that has never been connected to the grid. Officials in Dakar acknowledge that maintenance, not construction, remains the hardest part of the problem, and that the ministry has been slow to fund it. Two of the four districts have since asked the ministry for extra money to replace the pumps altogether.

The economics are awkward. A new borehole costs several times what a repair does, yet repairs are the first line to be cut when budgets tighten, and a pump that fails in August may not be fixed until March. Aid agencies have long argued that the answer lies in spare parts and trained mechanics rather than in concrete, though the political appeal of a ribbon-cutting has not diminished. Villagers here say they would settle for a mechanic within walking distance.

The regional water authority says it will publish a full audit before the end of the year, comparing costs across the four districts that took part and setting out which repairs held up after the first rainy season. The audit will also publish, for the first time, the response times logged by the district workshops. Researchers at the university have already begun a parallel study, tracking water quality at forty sites and interviewing households about how the time saved is spent.

That question matters more than it might seem. Where the walk to water fell by half, school attendance among girls rose by nearly a fifth, according to preliminary figures. The pumps themselves are unremarkable: cast iron, a metre tall, bolted to a concrete pad, with a handle worn smooth by years of use. What changed was the distance between the water and the people who needed it.
